paper_title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Predicting how actions affect the physical world and learning to generate actions are closely related problems [1]. World models predict future observations from specified actions [2, 3], while world-action models (WAMs) use video generation to guide action generation [4, 5]. These complementary objectives motivate studying world and action modeling within unified framework. Video foundation models support policy learning by predicting future observations [46]. One line of work [79] uses mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architectures [10], in which action tokens attend to bidirectional video representations [1, 1113]. These visual representations serve as effective policy priors and support strong manipulation performance. Related studies [2, 8, 14, 15] jointly model video and action generation within shared architectures, further demonstrating how video generation benefits action learning. In parallel, causal WAMs [5, 16, 17] use directional attention to couple video and action generation, aiming to capture causal dynamics in more physically consistent way. These results demonstrate the value of video prediction for action learning, yet the interaction between action-conditioned world modeling and action generation under temporal causality warrants further study. With bidirectional backbones augmented with an action-inference branch, the video branch often retains its pretrained attention [7], reflecting the Equal contribution. Corresponding authors. Figure 1: Action conditioning for world and action modeling. Rows denote queries and columns denote keys/values. Vc, V1,2, and A1,2 represent visual context, future video, and aligned actions, respectively. Outlined blocks compare world prediction conditioned on clean ground-truth actions (solid orange) with WAM prediction using noisy actions (hatching) or masked action keys (light gray). Percentages indicate the fraction of clean ground-truth actions. OneWM (blue) mixes all-clean, partial-clean, and all-noisy examples to examine whether world and action modeling benefit each other under unified causal training. premise that existing visual representations suffice as policy priors. Causal WAMs allow video tokens to attend to actions, but these actions are noisy variables under joint denoising [5, 17]. Joint generation therefore differs from forward dynamics prediction conditioned on specified clean actions. Conditioning video generation on ground-truth actions makes forward dynamics an explicit learning objective, raising our first question: Can learning such action-conditioned forward dynamics improve action learning within the same causal model? Within the same framework, action generation may in turn provide learning signal for visual prediction, motivating the converse question: Can learning to generate actions, in turn, improve action-conditioned world modeling within the same causal model? Existing architectures provide straightforward basis for unified causal training, allowing us to investigate these questions within shared model. In causal MoT framework, Fig. 1 illustrates two endpoints: an all-clean setting, where world model predicts video conditioned on clean ground-truth actions, and an all-noisy setting, where noisy action tokens serve as generation targets while conditioning video prediction. The figure also shows an representative WAM formulation that prevents video tokens from attending to action tokens. Both WAM formulations are organized around action generation through denoising, limiting action-to-video information flow: the video branch receives only noisy actions or no action information at all. To connect explicit forward-dynamics learning with action generation, we consider OneWM, unified causal model that supports both all-clean and all-noisy conditioning, together with partial-clean setting, which uses clean action prefix to condition both future-video prediction and denoising of the remaining noisy suffix. Each training batch mixes the three settings, enabling us to examine reciprocal benefits between forward-dynamics learning and action generation within the same causal model. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple simulated and real-world environments to examine whether world and action modeling benefit each other under unified causal training. Our results provide positive answers to both questions. First, under OneWMs unified causal training, incorporating clean-action conditioning into world model learning substantially improves the policys action-prediction performance, outperforming the evaluated WAMs with action-masked or noisy-action-conditioned video branches. Second, learning to generate actions also improves actionconditioned world modeling, showing that the benefits can be reciprocal in this setting. We further analyze the interaction between the two learning tasks.

sections.title: 2.1 World Action Models
sections.content: World-action models bring predictive world representations into policy learning. One line of work uses generated videos as visual plans or synthetic demonstrations, recovering executable actions through inverse dynamics or goalconditioned controllers [1820]. Other approaches integrate visual forecasting into the policy itself, using predictive video features [2123] or jointly learning future observations and actions [46, 9, 2426]. These formulations use temporal supervision and video pretraining to improve policy generalization and data efficiency. Recent work also separates predictive learning from the cost of future synthesis. Efficient WAMs retain video co-training while reducing or bypassing future-video generation at deployment [7, 27]. Latent and condition-space approaches couple future-representation prediction with action generation [2830], while representation distillation transfers worldmodel features to policies without adding generative process at inference [31]. We build on these predictive approaches by making the visual consequences of specified actions an explicit learning target during policy training.

sections.title: 2.2 World Models
sections.content: World models learn transition dynamics for planning and policy optimization, either in compact latent spaces [3234] or through visual forecasting [35, 36]. Large-scale video pretraining provides reusable visual dynamics priors [1, 13], while robotic world models develop control interfaces that relate these priors to concrete robot commands. Frame-level action injection and spatially grounded kinematic conditioning support fine-grained, controllable rollouts [3739]. Latent-action pretraining offers complementary route to learning interaction dynamics from unlabeled videos before adapting to robot controls [40, 41]. These predictors increasingly serve as learned simulators for policy evaluation and improvement, supplying imagined rollouts and synthetic experience [3, 38, 42, 43]. Their dynamics priors can also be transferred directly to policy learning [44]. These applications require predictions that follow the supplied actions, property distinguished from visual plausibility in recent evaluations [45]. Our work also treats actions as learning targets, using action-generation supervision to strengthen the representations underlying these predictions.

sections.title: 2.3 Unified World and Action Modeling
sections.content: Unified models support world prediction and action generation through shared representations and flexible conditioning [2, 8, 14, 15]. This line spans bidirectional diffusion frameworks [6, 15] and causal designs with autoregressive or directional information flow [5, 16, 17]. Existing studies report both reciprocal benefits and task trade-offs. For example, WorldVLA [46] interleaves discrete image and action tokens in shared autoregressive model, coupling action generation with action-conditioned nextimage prediction. Joint training improves both action generation and long-horizon visual prediction. By contrast, Cosmos 3 [15] reports that joint learning with video improves action prediction under bidirectional videoaction diffusion, but co-training with action prediction leads to small decline in video-generation fidelity. These findings arise from different modeling settings: WorldVLA demonstrates mutual benefits through discrete autoregressive imageaction modeling, whereas Cosmos 3 studies joint videoaction learning with bidirectional attention. Together, they leave open how temporal causality shapes the learning of physical dynamics and the resulting benefits for video and action prediction. We investigate this interaction within shared causal videoaction MoT framework, explicitly coupling action-conditioned forward-dynamics learning with action generation to examine their reciprocal benefits.

sections.title: 3.2 Temporally Causal Video--Action Modeling
sections.content: To examine the interaction between forward-dynamics learning and action learning, OneWM couples the two tasks through common causal MoT backbone [10]  (Fig. 2)  . We initialize the video expert from pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V5B [13] and reuse its video VAE and text encoder. The video expert models visual dynamics in latent space, and the action expert models action chunks. Modality-specific attention projections and feed-forward layers accommodate their different representations. Both experts receive the instruction ℓ through separate text cross-attention modules, allowing the same task semantics to condition visual prediction and action generation. The causal structure is specified by the temporal alignment of video and action blocks. Let V0 denote the observed visual context, Vi the tokens of future latent frame i, and Ai the action segment aligned with that frame. Thus, future video queries access the video and action prefixes up to their aligned block, while action queries use the observed visual context and the corresponding action prefix. Context queries remain confined to the observation stream. Tokens within future frame or an action segment can interact freely, and dependencies between blocks follow temporal order. Following MoT, the experts use their own query, key, and value projections while performing joint attention over the permitted tokens. The aggregated features Um are then processed by the corresponding experts output projection and remaining layers. This asymmetric coupling connects the two learning tasks under temporal causality. Attention to action features grounds forward-dynamics prediction in control signals, while attention to the observed video features supports action generation. Both objectives train the interconnected experts, providing routes for learning signals from one task to shape representations used by the other. Across the training regimes described next, we retain these visibility relations and vary which actions serve as clean conditions or prediction targets. This allows us to study the interaction between the two learning objectives within the same causal architecture.

sections.title: 3.5 Inference
sections.content: We use two inference settings corresponding to the all-clean and all-noisy endpoints in Sec. 3.3. Sampling integrates the velocity fields learned in Sec. 3.4 from noise (τ = 1) to clean outputs (τ = 0), with the observed visual context and language instruction held fixed. World prediction. The action chunk is supplied as clean conditioning (r = K) and remains fixed throughout sampling. The video expert denoises future video latents initialized from Gaussian noise, conditioned on = (zctx, ℓ)the observed visual context and language instructiontogether with the specified actions. The video VAE decodes the resulting latents into predicted frames. Action generation. The action chunk is initialized from Gaussian noise (r = 0) and denoised by the action expert, conditioned on the same observed visual context and language instruction. Observed video representations are reused across denoising steps. For closed-loop control, new action chunk is generated from the latest observations at each replanning step.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks and evaluation. We evaluate on three simulation benchmarks: LIBERO [48], LIBERO-Plus [49] for generalization under diverse perturbations, and RoboCasa365 [50] for mobile manipulation in complex environments. Real-world experiments cover block stacking, block insertion, and breakfast arrangement  (Fig. 3)  . We report task success rates for policy evaluation and PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and FVD for world prediction. Detailed training and evaluation protocols are provided in Appendix A. Comparisons. To answer our first questionwhether learning action-conditioned forward dynamics improves action learningwe compare OneWM with the two WAM variants illustrated in Fig. 1. The action-masked WAM (WAMmask) prevents future-video tokens from attending to action tokens, blocking action-to-video information flow. The noisy-action-conditioned WAM (WAMnoisy) allows such attention but conditions video prediction on noisy actions throughout training. Both jointly learn video and action prediction; OneWM additionally trains with clean and partially clean actions. To answer our second questionwhether learning to generate actions improves action-conditioned world modelingwe compare OneWM with the world-model baseline (WM). Corresponding to the all-clean setting in Fig. 1, WM predicts future video conditioned on clean actions without an action-prediction objective.

sections.title: 4.2 World Modeling for Action Learning
sections.content: To address our first question, we compare the policies learned by OneWM and the two WAM variants under the same causal architecture. All three jointly learn video and action prediction, while OneWM also learns forward dynamics conditioned on clean actions. This comparison tests whether explicitly learning the visual consequences of specified actions benefits action learning. In-distribution performance and generalization. OneWM outperforms both WAM variants on in-distribution LIBERO and out-of-distribution LIBERO-Plus  (Table 1)  . On LIBERO, the gains span spatial, object, and long-horizon tasks, while goal performance matches the stronger variant. On LIBERO-Plus, the advantages extend to background, camera, language, layout, and sensor-noise perturbations, with particularly strong gains under sensor noise. Camera and layout changes require the policy to adapt to different visual configurations while preserving the intended interaction. 7 The improvements in these settings suggest that learning action-conditioned dynamics strengthens representations of task-relevant scene changes. The benefit remains uneven under lighting changes and robot initialization. The comparison with Fast-WAM further highlights this generalization advantage. Although OneWM trails Fast-WAM on LIBERO, it outperforms it across all LIBERO-Plus perturbation categories and achieves the best overall result among the listed policies. Fast-WAM [7] uses bidirectional attention within its video and action experts while separating future-video prediction from action generation. In OneWM, clean-action conditioning and causal joint attention ground video prediction in specified controls and their temporal order. This supervision encourages the visual expert to capture how actions change object configurations, shaping the observed representations used by the action expert. The stronger performance under distribution shift is consistent with learning transferable interaction dynamics rather than relying primarily on correlations specific to familiar scenes. Manipulation in diverse scenes. On RoboCasa365, OneWM surpasses WAMmask and the listed reference policies across all task groups. The benchmark spans stationary and mobile manipulation across diverse scene layouts, object arrangements, and articulated fixtures [50]. Many tasks involve base motion, which adds viewpoint changes to the spatial changes caused by manipulation. Learning action-conditioned forward dynamics encourages the visual expert to track how controls change these objectscene relationships. The policy gains are consistent with this supervision providing richer spatial representations for manipulation in more complex and changing scenes.

Stacking tests relative placement, insertion tests precise alignment, and breakfast arrangement tests successive manipulations as the scene changes. OneWM improves over WAMmask on all three tasks  (Fig. 4)  , especially insertion and breakfast arrangement. Whereas WAMmask excludes actions from video prediction, OneWM learns their visual consequences. These results answer our first question affirmatively: explicitly learning forward dynamics conditioned on clean actions improves action learning within the same causal model. Both WAM variants already receive future-video supervision, so the gains highlight the additional value of learning how specified controls change the scene. This benefit carries over to deployment, where the policy generates actions from noise. The stronger performance across scene perturbations and complex interactions suggests that clean-action world modeling shapes representations of robotscene dynamics that remain useful when future controls must be inferred, supporting policy generalization across changing visual configurations.

sections.title: 4.3 Action Learning for World Modeling
sections.content: We next address our second question: whether action learning improves action-conditioned world modeling. We compare OneWM with WM, which uses the same MoT architecture but learns only future-video prediction conditioned on clean actions, without an action-prediction objective. Both receive clean action chunks at inference. To distinguish joint attention from action modulation, we also design an IRASim-inspired [37] world-model baseline, WMAdaLN, that injects action conditions through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN). It uses the same Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone as our MoT models. Table 2 additionally includes Wan [13] as video-prediction reference. 8 Table 2: World-prediction performance. Since the two models share the MoT architecture, this pattern supports the benefit of adding action learning to world-model training. Predicting actions requires the observed representation to capture the robotobject configurations relevant to control. This complementary supervision can strengthen the scene and forward-dynamics representations used to predict the visual consequences of specified actions. The improvements across pixel accuracy, structural similarity, and perceptual correspondence are consistent with this richer understanding of action-dependent scene changes. Strong prediction across complementary metrics. Compared with WM using the same MoT architecture, OneWM consistently improves paired prediction quality and FVD across the three benchmarks, as well as FID on LIBEROPlus and RoboCasa365. As the architecture-matched comparison, this fact provides clear evidence for the benefit of adding action learning. OneWM ranks first or second on every metric across the three benchmarks, with the modulation-based WMAdaLN achieving higher performance on FID/FVD in some settingsan advantage in matching feature distributions also observed over the MoT-based WM. Paired prediction metrics and distributional metrics characterize complementary aspects of world modeling: the former measure agreement with the reference outcome under given conditioning sequence, while FID and FVD compare marginal feature distributions without explicitly evaluating actionoutcome correspondence [37, 54, 55]. Appendix further evaluates this correspondence through local geometry and action-dependent motion in externaland wrist-camera predictions across all three benchmarks. These results answer our second question affirmatively: action learning improves the prediction of specified-action outcomes under identical clean-action inference conditions. Learning to generate actions gives the shared model additional supervision for robotobject relationships relevant to control. This complementary signal can strengthen the scene representations used to predict the visual consequences of specified actions. Together with Sec. 4.2, the results suggest reciprocal role for the two objectives: forward prediction learns how controls change scene, while action generation emphasizes the scene structure needed to choose them. Both can strengthen the same representations of interaction under unified causal training.

sections.title: 4.4 Effect of the Action-Conditioning Mixture
sections.content: The preceding sections examine the two directions of transfer separately. We now consider how the conditioning mixture in Sec. 3.3 affects both tasks. We vary the sampling probabilities of all-noisy, partial-clean, and all-clean examples, comparing 60/25/15, 50/35/15, and 30/45/25. Table 3 reports policy success alongside world-prediction quality; the inference settings remain those in Sec. 3.5. Policy performance and world-prediction quality remain broadly stable between 60/25/15 and 50/35/15. The modest shift toward partial-clean conditioning brings small in-distribution policy gain, while the default remains stronger on LIBERO-Plus and paired prediction metrics. Joint visual and action learning is therefore reasonably stable to moderate changes in the mixture. larger shift toward clean conditioning leaves world-prediction metrics relatively stable but weakens policy performance, particularly under distribution shift. This pattern suggests that policy generalization benefits from preserving sufficient all-noisy training, which matches deployment where actions are generated from noise. sections.title: 4.5 Endless Dream: Closing the Loop in Imagination
sections.content: Beyond the improvements above, the two inference modes in Sec. 3.5 can compose into an endless dream: OneWM alternates action generation and action-conditioned world prediction, using each imagined outcome as the context for its next decision. Let ˆo0 be the initial multi-view observation and Cj = (E(ˆoj), ℓ) the context at round j, where and denote the video VAE encoder and decoder. The loop is ˆaj pθ(a Cj), ˆoj+1 = last(cid:0)D(ˆzfut )(cid:1) . pθ(zfut Cj, ˆaj), ˆzfut (6) Both stages use the same model: the action chunk is first denoised from noise, then held fixed as clean conditioning for video generation. The final predicted frame from each camera is fed back into the next round, with the instruction unchanged and no further environment observations. On LIBERO tasks, we run this loop for 16 rounds without additional training. Each round generates 32 actions and eight future frames, yielding 512 actions over modeled horizon of 25.6 seconds. The resulting sequences show task-directed progression through drawer opening, pushing, and singleand multi-object transport (Appendix C). This composability connects the two learned capabilities beyond separate evaluation: action generation selects controls from imagined states, while forward prediction supplies the states on which subsequent decisions depend.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We studied whether world and action modeling can benefit each other under unified causal training. OneWM combines clean-action-conditioned forward prediction and action generation in causal MoT model by mixing all-clean, partialclean, and all-noisy examples. Controlled simulation comparisons provide positive answers to both questions: explicit forward-dynamics learning improves policy performance and generalization, while action learning improves actionconditioned world prediction within the same architecture. Real-world manipulation further validates the policy benefit. These results suggest that the two objectives supervise complementary aspects of interaction: the visual consequences of controls and the scene structure needed to select them. The mixture study shows that this benefit tolerates moderate rebalancing, while larger shifts toward clean conditioning mainly weaken policy generalization. OneWM thus supports learning world prediction and control through mutually beneficial representations under temporal causality. These findings motivate studying how reciprocal learning scales with more diverse data and longer interaction horizons. further direction is to use the learned dynamics for planning and policy improvement, extending the interaction between prediction and control beyond joint training.

sections.title: A Training and Evaluation Protocols
sections.content: A.1 Training and Deployment Simulation training. For LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, we adopt the LIBERO training recipe of Fast-WAM [7]. We train jointly on demonstrations from the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites for 20 epochs with global batch size of 128. The resulting models are evaluated on LIBERO-Plus directly. For RoboCasa365, we train on its demonstration dataset for 90k optimizer steps with global batch size of 1024. Real-world training. We collect 50 demonstrations for each of the three real-world tasks: block stacking, block insertion, and breakfast arrangement, yielding 150 episodes in total. Models are trained on these demonstrations for 20 epochs with global batch size of 96. Internal comparisons. All internal WAM and WM ablations follow the same dataset-specific training protocol, including training data, global batch size, and training budget. Their action conditioning and learning objectives differ as described in Sec. 4.1. Unless otherwise stated, OneWM samples all-noisy, partial-clean, and all-clean action conditioning with probabilities 60%, 25%, and 15%, respectively. Deployment. Following Sec. 3.5, policies generate action chunks from Gaussian noise using the current visual observations and language instruction. Observed video representations are reused during action denoising, without generating future video. For world prediction, the specified action chunk remains clean and fixed while the model denoises future video latents. A.2 Evaluation Protocols Policy evaluation. We measure closed-loop task success using each benchmarks success criterion. LIBERO results cover the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites and their average; LIBERO-Plus results cover the seven perturbation categories and the benchmark aggregate. RoboCasa365 results are reported for atomic-seen, composite-seen, and composite-unseen tasks. Each real-world task is evaluated over 15 trials per model, with success rates reported as percentages. Inference follows Sec. 3.5. Video evaluation. LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 are designed for policy evaluation and do not provide dedicated validation sets for action-conditioned video prediction. We therefore construct evaluation video sets from expert rollouts. For LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, we collect 100 complete episodes in total using π0.5 [52], uniformly sampling across LIBERO settings and LIBERO-Plus perturbation categories. For RoboCasa365, we collect 100 complete episodes with Xiaomi-Robotics-1 [56], uniformly sampling its 50 evaluation target tasks. All three benchmarks are evaluated with multi-view future predictions, including external-camera and wrist-camera observations. Prediction chunks span 32 action steps with frame-sampling stride of 4 for LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and 16 action steps with stride of 2 for RoboCasa365. Each chunk thus evaluates eight future frames, excluding the conditioning frames. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed from losslessly stored RGB frames scaled to [0, 1] using PIQ 0.8 [57]. For FID and FVD, both predictions and references are encoded with H.264 at constant quantization parameter 20 in YUV420p format and decoded before feature extraction. PSNR. Peak signal-to-noise ratio measures pixel reconstruction accuracy as 10 log10(MSE + 108) in decibels, where MSE is averaged over RGB channels and pixels. Higher is better. SSIM. Structural similarity [58] compares local luminance, contrast, and structure. We use PIQs single-scale implementation with an 11 11 Gaussian window, standard deviation 1.5, unit data range, and K1 = 0.01, K2 = 0.03. Higher is better. LPIPS. Learned perceptual image patch similarity [59] measures perceptual distance using PIQs ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 backbone, learned calibration weights, and default input normalization. Lower is better. FID. Fréchet Inception Distance [54] compares generated and reference image-feature distributions using 2,048dimensional average-pooling features from PIQs TensorFlow-compatible Inception-v3. Frames are bilinearly resized to 299 299 and normalized to [1, 1]. Lower is better. FVD. Our Fréchet Video Distance [55] implementation uses 400-dimensional output logits from PyTorchVideos I3D-R50 pretrained on Kinetics-400. Each clip contains eight future frames in temporal order, bilinearly resized to 224 224 and normalized from [0, 1] with channel-wise mean 0.45 and standard deviation 0.225. Lower is better. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are averaged over all evaluated future frames. FID and FVD use feature means and covariances pooled over each benchmark to compute the Fréchet distance, rather than averaging per-batch scores. 17 Qualitative Analysis of Action-Conditioned World Prediction We inspect selected, matched prediction windows from the evaluated model variants on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365. Each comparison uses the same observed context, instruction, clean action sequence, and camera. The figures show four future frames and shared-coordinate detail at the final time step. Main-camera predictions. Figure 5 highlights spatial relationships at the scene level. Compared with WMAdaLN, OneWM more closely follows the held moka pot and gripper pose in (a), the grippers position relative to the cream cheese box in (b), and the gripper height near the sauce bottle in (c). Comparisons with WM show closer correspondence in the bottle rotation (d), cartonbasket alignment (e), and gripperplate relationship (f). These examples illustrate the value of action learning for representing how robot motion changes the scene configuration. Figure 5: Main-camera world predictions. Six cases from LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus compare GT, OneWM, and the indicated world-model baseline. Orange boxes mark the regions enlarged at + 32 in each panels final column. 18 Wrist-camera predictions. Figure 6 reveals local geometry during interaction. Against WMAdaLN, OneWM better preserves the drawers image position in (a), the cream cheese box near the gripper in (b), and the sauce caps position and orientation in (c). Against WM, it better retains the visible bottle-neck geometry in (d), the butter packages extent in (e), and the bottle inclination in (f). The cream cheese, sauce, and wine cases also appear in the main view, allowing the same predictions to be inspected from complementary cameras. Figure 6: Wrist-camera world predictions. Six matched comparisons emphasize object position, shape, and pose near the gripper. Each final column enlarges the same marked region at + 32 for all three rows. Conditional fidelity and distributional quality. These examples help interpret the different metric rankings in Table 2. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS compare each prediction with its corresponding reference, whereas FID and FVD compare pooled feature statistics [54, 55]. Reassigning generated clips to different action sequences would leave these pooled statistics unchanged. lower distributional distance therefore need not imply more accurate action-conditioned geometry. 19 RoboCasa365 predictions. Figure 7 extends the comparisons to diverse scenes across three camera views. In the left views (a,b), OneWM more closely tracks forearm withdrawal and gripperdoor motion. In the wrist views (c,d), the baselines overpredict viewpoint change, shifting the fridge geometry and bringing the bowl into view too early. The right views (e,f) show closer correspondence in gripper descent and orientation near the counter and ice cube. These differences concern motion relative to scene structure, rather than appearance alone, illustrating the value of action learning for conditional spatial prediction. Figure 7: RoboCasa365 world predictions. Six matched cases compare GT, OneWM, WM, and WMAdaLN from left (a,b), wrist (c,d), and right (e,f) cameras. The final column enlarges the same marked region at + 16 for all four rows.

sections.title: C Endless Dream on LIBERO
sections.content: We instantiate the loop in Eq. 6 with the jointly trained LIBERO model and the default conditioning mixture. Each rollout starts from one main-camera image, one wrist-camera image, and task instruction. Both inference stages use 10 denoising steps with fixed seed of 42. The generated action chunk is passed unchanged to world prediction; its final multi-view prediction becomes the next visual context. Only the initial observation is obtained from the environment. All rollouts use fixed budget of 16 rounds, with 32 actions and eight predicted frames per round. Figure 8 shows intermediate states and the final state of every rollout. Figure 8: Endless dream on LIBERO. Six rollouts generated by alternating action prediction and action-conditioned world prediction. Each panel shows mainand wrist-camera views; blue outlines mark the initial observations, and every later frame is generated. Columns indicate modeled time, with the final column showing the end of round 16.
